lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Anna and Luke, discussing their research for a project on packaging. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: OK, Luke, shall we go through what we've found for the packaging project? The presentation's on Thursday, so we haven't got long.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: Sure. I've read a lot more than I expected to. I hadn't realised how confusing the words on packaging are.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: You mean 'biodegradable' and 'compostable'? I know. Before this project I'd have said they were exactly the same thing.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: And so would most shoppers, I think. In the survey we did outside the supermarket, nearly everyone thought the two words meant the same.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: But they don't. Compostable packaging has to break down within a fixed time in the right conditions. 'Biodegradable' doesn't promise any time at all. In theory, almost anything biodegrades in the end.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: Right. And I was surprised there's no single legal definition of 'biodegradable'. I'd assumed it was strictly controlled.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: Me too. Some people argue 'biodegradable' is the more useful label, because it's the one everybody recognises, but I don't agree. It tells you almost nothing.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: The thing that worried me most was something I read about behaviour. When people see the word 'biodegradable', some of them think it doesn't matter if they drop the packaging in the street or put it in any bin.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: Yes, because they think it'll just disappear. So the label can actually make people more careless.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: Exactly. Mind you, I wouldn't go as far as saying companies should stop using the words. They just need to explain them properly.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: Agreed. Now, what about paper? A lot of companies are switching from plastic to paper, and they make some big claims about it.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: Well, some of the claims are fair. Paper comes from trees, and trees can be replanted, so it is a renewable material. I've no problem with that one.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: No. But the claim that paper always takes less energy to make than plastic is just wrong. A paper bag needs much more energy and water to produce than a thin plastic one.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: That's right. You'd have to use a paper bag several times to make up for it, and most people use them once.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: And paper can be recycled several times, which is true, so that's a real advantage.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: It is. But I don't accept the idea that paper breaks down quickly in landfill. Landfill sites are tightly packed, with hardly any air, so paper can stay there for decades. People have dug up newspapers you could still read.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: That's amazing. And what about the claim that customers think paper looks better quality? I think that's probably true. Our survey showed that, didn't it?

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: Yes, most people said paper made a product feel more natural and better quality. So that's fine.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Now look at questions 25 to 30.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: Shall we move on to the newer materials? I think they'll be the most interesting part of the presentation.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: Definitely. Let's start with mushroom packaging. That's the one I find the most amazing.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: It's made from mycelium, isn't it? The root-like part of a fungus.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: Yes. They mix it with farm waste and put it into moulds, and in about a week it grows to fill the mould. So you can grow it into exactly the shape you need to protect a product.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: Brilliant. Then there's seaweed. I read that seaweed film is completely safe to eat, so you could swallow the wrapper along with the food inside.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: And I like the fact that seaweed doesn't need any fresh water or fertiliser to grow, unlike a lot of crops.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: What about bagasse? I'd never even heard of it before.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: It's the dry fibre that's left over after sugar cane has been crushed to get the juice out. It used to be burnt or thrown away, but now it's pressed into plates and takeaway boxes.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: I like that it uses waste. Now, the cornstarch plastic is the one I'm least sure about. It looks just like normal plastic.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: It's called PLA. It's made from plants, which sounds good, but it won't break down in a garden compost heap. It needs the high temperatures of an industrial composting plant, and there aren't many of those.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: So in most places it just ends up with ordinary rubbish. OK. And recycled cardboard. Everyone thinks that's the perfect solution.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: It's good, but it isn't perfect. Each time paper is recycled, the fibres get shorter, so the cardboard gets weaker. After five or six times, the fibres are too short to use.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: And finally glass. I was expecting it to be expensive, but it's actually quite cheap to produce.

lines.speaker: LUKE
lines.text: And it can be recycled again and again without losing quality. The problem is that it's so heavy. Moving it around in lorries burns a lot more fuel than lighter materials.

lines.speaker: ANNA
lines.text: Good. I think we've got enough for the main part. Shall we start on the slides?

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 3.

Companies should stop using them on packaging.
